# Explain the DockLayouts gesture and commit mechanics

## Context

The existing DockLayouts guide gives one concise gesture walkthrough, but the final package now separates interaction, model, and projection responsibilities across `src/dashboard/dock/{interaction,model,projection}/`. Readers still lack a deep explanation of how a physical gesture becomes exactly one semantic commit and a reconciled projection.

## The Problem

An adopter or maintainer must currently reconstruct threshold crossing, claim ownership, preview production, cancellation, operation emission, reducer commit, and projection reconciliation from source and tests. That is the subsystem's most important behavioral loop, and a shallow overview cannot explain why cancellation, stale generations, or rejected moves must commit nothing.

## The Architectural Reality

`interaction/DockSplitter.mjs`, `TabSortZone.mjs`, `PreviewProducer.mjs`, `model/Operations.mjs`, `model/Document.mjs`, `projection/Reconciler.mjs`, and `Workspace.mjs` form the current authority chain. Generic pointer/drag machinery remains below DockLayouts; dock interactions add semantic descriptors rather than a second drag engine.

## The Fix

Create `learn/guides/uibuildingblocks/DockLayoutsMechanics.md`: a narrative guide that follows representative split resize, tab movement, and edge resize gestures from pointer intent through commit and re-projection, including the failure paths that preserve prior truth.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The guide clears the full guide-authoring bar: source/tool-grounded narrative, reader-owned benefits, lived maintainer voice, and at least one render-verified `flowchart TD`.
- [ ] The guide separates explanation from reference: no inlined API/schema/test catalog, and no ticket or PR ids in guide prose.
- [ ] The new source guide is registered in `learn/tree.json` and the SEO `PRIORITIES` input; generated sitemap/LLM outputs remain untouched.
- [ ] Current-source consistency, guide lint, tree lint, portal rendering, and an independent cross-family whole-guide review are recorded in the PR.
- [ ] At least three real gesture families are traced, including one rejected/cancelled arm and their exact state/ownership transitions.
- [ ] The story distinguishes physical pixels, runtime preview state, semantic descriptors, committed documents, and projected component state.
- [ ] The author exercises the current Workstation/example gesture path rather than writing from source inference alone.

## Out of Scope

API reference tables, exhaustive operation schemas, feature marketing, or changing DockLayouts behavior.

## Avoided Traps

Do not duplicate the intro's short walkthrough, teach DOM mutation as authority, or present every source class as a chapter.

## Intake revalidation at `dev@cce07cdade` — boundary holds, naming drift only

Picking this up. Per the Activation Gate, the boundary was re-read against current source before any prose:

- **`model/Document.mjs` no longer exists.** The committed-document contract — schema keys, validation, normalization, tree helpers and the fail-closed commit — now lives in `model/WorkspaceDocument.mjs`, split out of the former monolithic zone model.
- **The chain has two owners the body does not name.** `interaction/DragAffordances.mjs` is the per-workspace gesture controller: once-per-gesture memoized geometry, the indicator-first preview consumer and the release-truth drop, with `clear()` invalidating every in-flight await. `model/PreviewContract.mjs` owns preview validation and conversion.
- **Not every commit runs through `Neo.manager.Transaction`.** The Workspace commits through `applyDockZoneOperation` and loads the transaction manager lazily, only once a Group or tear-out lifecycle needs it; a standalone workspace never loads it. The guide will say that rather than draw every gesture through the Group.

`DockSplitter`, `TabSortZone`, `PreviewProducer`, `Operations`, `Reconciler` and `Workspace` are all present. The proposed split — one gesture pipeline and its zero-commit failure paths, distinct from state/persistence and window lifecycles — still fits, so no reshape.
